title: Claude gets its own browser in Cowork
content:
Claude gets its own browser in Cowork
Claude opens its own browser to navigate sites, read pages, and fill forms, inside the desktop app.
Claude now has a browser built into Claude Cowork on the desktop app. When a task needs to use a website, a browser opens in the side panel and Claude navigates webpages, reads them, clicks, and types. You can now hand off the web part of the task and stay where you are: Claude can fill in a form, pull numbers from a dashboard, or work through a portal that has no connector. No extension, no setup, and nothing shared from your own browser unless you choose to.
Until now, giving Claude the ability to use the web in Cowork meant giving it access to your browser through the Claude in Chrome extension. When the work is on a page you already have open, that's still the right choice. But a lot of web tasks don't need your browser, just a browser, and now Claude has one.
It's rolling out this week to Pro, Max, and Team plans in the Claude desktop app. Enterprise admins can turn it on for their organization starting today.
It's Claude's browser, not yours. The built-in browser is separate from your own. Claude never sees your tabs, bookmarks, or passwords. To stay signed in to your sites, you can bring your logins over site by site, from Chrome, Edge, or Firefox on macOS and from Firefox on Windows and Linux. Banking, email, and single sign-on sites are left out unless you choose to include them.
That's also the difference between the two ways Claude can use the web. The built-in browser is for handing web tasks to Claude while you keep working: gathering research for a report, or collecting this month’s invoices from a vendor portal. Claude in Chrome is for the page you already have open, with the accounts you're already signed in to, such as updating your CRM, working through your inbox, or editing the doc in front of you.
If you already use Claude in Chrome, it keeps working and stays your default; otherwise Claude uses the built-in browser. Switch anytime in Settings → Cowork → Preferred browser.
The built-in browser carries the same prompt injection risks as any AI agent that acts in a browser, where instructions hidden in a page try to redirect Claude. It runs the same safeguards as Claude in Chrome, including the checks that review Claude's actions against what you asked for. We describe them on the Claude in Chrome blog post. Those measures meaningfully reduce the risk but can't eliminate it, so we recommend starting on sites you trust. Read our safety guide for more.
The built-in browser is rolling out over the coming week to Pro, Max, and Team plans in the Claude desktop app on macOS, Windows, and Linux (in beta). Once it reaches you, it's on by default: give Claude a task that involves a website and the browser opens on its own. On Enterprise plans, it's available now and admins can manage it in Organization settings → Cowork → Built-in browser.
The built-in browser lives in the desktop app. From the web or your phone, Claude can still drive it as long as your desktop app is open and online. On the web without the desktop app, Claude in Chrome remains the way to give Claude a browser.

report.summary: Claude desktop app adds a built-in browser in Cowork, letting Claude autonomously navigate websites and fill forms without your own browser.
report.background: Claude Cowork is Anthropic's agentic desktop environment where Claude can work alongside users on tasks. Previously, giving Claude web access in Cowork required the Claude in Chrome extension, which lets Claude use pages you already have open and signed in. That approach was good for tasks on current pages, but many tasks simply need a separate browser. The new built-in browser gives Claude its own isolated browsing environment inside the desktop app, automatically opening when a task involves websites. It can navigate, read, extract data, and fill forms. It is rolling out across paid plans, with enterprise controls, and includes privacy features like optional login import and exclusions for sensitive sites. The release reflects Anthropic's push toward more autonomous, agentic workflows while addressing security and data isolation concerns.
key_points: The Claude desktop app now includes a built-in browser inside Cowork, letting Claude open webpages, read content, click links, and fill forms on its own. This works directly in a side panel, requires no extension or setup, and triggers automatically when a task involves a website.

The built-in browser is separate from your personal browser. Claude cannot see your tabs, bookmarks, or passwords. You can import logins site by site from Chrome, Edge, or Firefox on macOS, and Firefox on Windows/Linux. Banking, email, and SSO sites are excluded unless you specifically include them.

This complements the existing Claude in Chrome extension. Use the extension for pages you already have open and are signed in to, like CRM or inbox tasks. The built-in browser handles standalone web tasks, such as research or pulling invoices, while you keep working. You can choose your preferred browser in Settings.

As with any AI browser agent, prompt injection is a risk—hidden instructions on a page might try to manipulate Claude. The built-in browser uses the same safeguards as Claude in Chrome, including checks against your requested task. Risks are reduced but not eliminated, so Anthropic recommends starting with trusted sites.

The feature is rolling out this week to Pro, Max, and Team plans in the desktop app on macOS, Windows, and Linux (beta). Enterprise administrators can enable it now. From the web or mobile, Claude can still control the built-in browser as long as the desktop app is open and online.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the built-in browser marks a shift from human-in-the-loop browsing to delegated agentic web access, competing with products like OpenAI's Operator while keeping execution inside a desktop app. Developers and power users gain a handy way to make Claude perform research, form filling, and data collection without exposing their personal browser or requiring custom connectors. Privacy-conscious users benefit because the browser is isolated, with optional per-site logins. However, the prompt-injection warning underscores that fully autonomous browsing remains risky. Enterprises get centralized control via admin settings, which may accelerate adoption in regulated environments where browser isolation is important.
report.tools: If you want to explore this further, watch Anthropic's Claude in Chrome extension for page-level work, and review the Claude in Chrome blog post and safety guide linked in the article. For open-source alternatives, see browser-use (Python library for AI browser agents) and Playwright MCP (Microsoft's browser automation for AI assistants).
